# Hierarchical Gating Network for Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation

SHULIANG WANG, JIABAO ZHU, and YI WANG , School of Computer Science

and Technology, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing, China

CHEN MA, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China

XIN ZHAO, School of Computer Science and Technology, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing, China YANSEN ZHANG, Department of Computer Science, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China ZIQIANG YUAN and SIJIE RUAN, School of Computer Science and Technology, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing, China

Cross-domain sequential recommendation (CDSR) utilizes data from multiple domains to recommend the user's next interaction based on his latest interaction sequence. Currently, many cross-domain sequential recommendation algorithms have been proven to achieve good recommendation performance. However, these algorithms overlook the influence of users' long-term behavioral patterns and general interests when extracting their current preferences. In this article, we propose a Hierarchical Gating Network for Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation (HGNCDSR). Specifically, we simultaneously train single-domain and cross-domain interaction sequences, utilizing a hierarchical gating network to capture user interest representations in single-domain and cross-domain, respectively. A feature gating and an instance gating are applied respectively to extract user interests at item feature level and instance level. While learning current preferences from behavior sequences, user representations that reflect behavioral patterns and general interests are simultaneously learned and strengthened. Additionally, we employ the item-item product to model the relationships between candidate items and those in the interaction sequence. Both current interests and item relevance are considered simultaneously, integrating single-domain and cross-domain user preferences to predict the user's next interaction. We design extensive experiments to show that HGNCDSR has better recommendation performance than other state-of-the-art models.

Syst. 43, 4, Article 90 (May 2025), 32 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3715321 ## 1 Introduction The rapid development of the Internet has led to significant information overload. To proactively identify and deliver content that aligns with user interests from vast amounts of data, recommendation systems have become a crucial research focus in the field of data mining. The primary objective of recommendation systems is to model a user's historical behavior data to extract their interests and preferences, thereby predicting future interactions. Over the past few decades, recommendation systems have evolved from traditional approaches such as collaborative filtering [42] to the integration of deep neural networks [40, 59], leading to notable performance improvements. The emergence of sequential recommendation [50,51] and cross-domain recommendation [57, 64] has further invigorated the field. Sequential recommendation algorithms account for the temporal dynamics of user behavior, capturing preferences that evolve over time, thereby enabling the recommendation of items that users are currently interested in and that reflect their recent activities. Cross-domain recommendation algorithms leverage historical behavior data across multiple domains, effectively addressing challenges like data sparsity \( \left\lbrack {{19},{35}}\right\rbrack \) and the cold-start problem \( \left\lbrack {1,2}\right\rbrack \) that traditional recommendation methods struggle to overcome. In order to further improve the personalization and accuracy of recommendation systems, many scholars have focused their research on the cross-domain sequential recommendation task in recent years [4, 9, 22, 31, 32, 58]. Cross-domain sequential recommendation combines the ideas of sequential recommendation and cross-domain recommendation, using multi-domain data to mine patterns in user's behavior sequences to provide personalized and accurate recommendation services. Therefore, how to capture the user's preferences based on the historical behavior sequence and how to combine user's historical behavior data from multiple domains are two key points in the cross-domain sequential recommendation task. Many scholars have proposed different solutions to the above two questions. For example, \( \pi \) -Net [32] generated the representations for the single-domain item sequences through the Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), and then transferred the single-domain representations between different domains through a gated transferring module. \( {C}^{2} \) DSR [4] utilized a graph and attention encoder to generate representations of single-domain and cross-domain sequences, leveraging contrastive learning to jointly learn and enhance single-domain and cross-domain user preferences. CMVCDR [58] learned the user's general interest representation through contrastive learning, which is divided into domain-invariant parts and domain-specific parts, and then utilized an attention mechanism based on item sequences to extract cross-domain knowledge related to domain-invariant factors to generate the user's current interest representation. Lin et al. [22] proposed a hybrid attention network (MAN) with local and global attention modules, which can be applied to the case of no overlapping users. Additionally, numerous researchers have also investigated the challenges of aligning and integrating information from different domains within cross-domain recommendation systems. For instance, Liu et al. [23] proposed a chiasmal embedding method for cross-domain knowledge graphs, which can effectively interact with items from multiple domains. Zhang et al. [60] introduced a deep cross-domain recommendation model, which employs two generators to construct a bi-directional personalized itemset mapping between users' behaviors in two different domains. Li et al. [21] proposed a Mutual Information-based preference separation and transfer framework that incorporates domain-shared preferences from different domains and integrates domain-specific preferences to improve recommendation.

The aforementioned algorithms have demonstrated effectiveness; however, they model user preferences solely based on the most recent item sequences with which the user has interacted, neglecting the influence of long-term behavioral patterns. Users with distinct behavioral patterns and general interests may exhibit different subsequent interactions, even after experiencing similar interaction sequences. For instance, some users prioritize the style of items, such as preferring suspense-themed books and movies, while others are more focused on the people associated with the items, like choosing to read books by specific authors or watch movies starring certain actors. As illustrated in Figure 1, both Mike and Bob recently watched Inception and Shutter Island. Mike chose these films due to his preference for suspense, leading him to watch The Sixth Sense next, another suspense movie. Conversely, Bob, who is a fan of Leonardo DiCaprio, the lead actor in both films, would likely watch Titanic next, which also stars DiCaprio. This example highlights that a user's personal traits are evident across their entire history of interactions and underscores the importance of considering general behavioral patterns and preferences when predicting future interactions based on recent activity. To deal with the problem mentioned above, we propose a Hierarchical Gating Network for Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation (HGNCDSR). Users' behavioral patterns and interest preferences are complex and varied, with both general and current preferences influencing the user's next interaction. Specifically, our model incorporates a feature gating module and an instance gating module, both linked to user representation, to extract personalized current interests. Concurrently, user representations are effectively learned and enhanced when extracting current interests from multiple item sequences over an extended period, thereby capturing users' general behavior patterns and interests. Additionally, we utilize the item-item product to model correlations between items. In the cross-domain scenario, we construct both single-domain and cross-domain item sequences by chronologically merging the data from individual domains. Since certain item features in a sequence can better reflect user preferences, and the impact of each item on predicting subsequent interactions varies, our model incorporates two gating mechanisms. The feature gating module filters the item features relevant to the user's preferences, while the instance gating module filters item instances that reflect the user's current interests. By employing these mechanisms, we extract interest representations for both single-domain and cross-domain contexts. Ultimately, the prediction of the user's next interaction is derived by integrating these interest representations with the correlations between candidate items and items in the user's historical interaction sequence.

The main contributions of this article are summarized below: - We propose a HGNCDSR, which jointly learns user representation, current interest representation, and item associations to more accurately model user behavior patterns and personalized interests. - We design a novel gating network that integrates feature gating and instance gating modules, enabling effective modeling of both long-term and short-term user behaviors. By capturing these patterns, the network generates accurate representations of users' current interests in both single-domain and cross-domain scenarios. This approach ensures that user interests in specific domains are effectively captured without compromising the chronological order of items across different domains. - We conduct four sets of comparative experiments in cross-domain scenarios using real-world datasets. Additionally, we design further experiments to validate the effectiveness of each module within our model and the overall rationality of our model framework. The experimental results demonstrate that HGNCDSR outperforms state-of-the-art methods. We have released the implementation codes for public use. \( {}^{1} \) ## 2 Related Work In this section, we introduce the related work of our work, including cross-domain recommendation, sequential recommendation and cross-domain sequential recommendation. ### 2.1 Cross-Domain Recommendation The goal of the cross-domain recommendation task is to leverage information from multiple related domains to improve recommendation performance in the target domain. Cross-domain recommendation was initially proposed to address challenges such as data sparsity and user cold-start, which traditional recommendation algorithms struggle to overcome, and has demonstrated promising results. The traditional cross-domain recommendation algorithms were developed from the single-domain recommendation algorithms [3, 26, 30, 44]. The main idea of these algorithms is to enrich user's interaction data by introducing other related domains. For example, Singh and Gordon [44] utilized the Collective Matrix Factorization technique to fuse relationship matrices from multiple domains into a shared low-dimensional latent space to simultaneously improve recommendation performance in multiple domains. Later, Ma et al. [30] proposed a factor analysis approach based on probabilistic matrix factorization which employs both users' social network information and rating records to solve the data sparsity and poor prediction accuracy problems. Cao et al. [3] proposed to utilize item similarity mining to solve the multi-market recommendation task. Later, transfer learning [34] was introduced into cross-domain recommendation. The main idea of this type of algorithms is to use neural networks to model user interest representation in each single-domain, and then transfer it between domains through a transferring module. For example, Man et al. [33] first proposed the EMCDR framework, which realizes knowledge transfer and recommendation between different domains by learning the representations of users and items in each single-domain and then mapping them. SSCDR [15] proposed a new cross-domain recommendation framework based on semi-supervised mapping, which can achieve good results even when there are only a few common users between domains. Hu et al. [14] proposed the CoNet model, which introduces cross-connections from one basic network to another to achieve cross-domain dual knowledge transfer. DDTCDR [20] designed a latent orthogonal mapping to extract user preferences on multiple domains while preserving the relationships between users in different latent spaces. Zhao et al. [62] proposed the CATN model, which utilizes an aspect transfer network to capture users' multi-faceted preferences in two relevant domains. --- \( {}^{1} \) https://github.com/solozhu/hgncdsr. ---

Recent advancements in cross-domain recommendation have concentrated on how to transfer user interests between different domains in a personalized manner and how to extract and transfer shareable information across domains. To enable personalized transfer of user interests, PTUPCDR [65] introduced a meta-network designed to generate individualized bridge functions for each user. Liu et al. [24] proposed the BiTGCF model, which leverages common users as a bridge to facilitate bidirectional knowledge transfer between two domains, integrating both shared user characteristics and domain-specific features in the transfer process. DisenCDR [5] introduced two disentanglement regularizers based on mutual information to separate domain-shared information from domain-specific details. Chen and Lee [7] developed CD-ELR, a model that communicates information across domains by combining matrix factorization with Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). Su et al. [45] proposed a Dual Adversarial Adaptation framework that adversarially trains the target model alongside a pre-trained source model, enabling the simultaneous learning of transferable domain-invariant features and target-domain-specific information. ### 2.2 Sequential Recommendation The sequential recommendation task aims to predict the next item a user will interact with by analyzing their behavior sequence and accounting for the dynamic changes in their interactions over time. This approach enables a more accurate capture of users' evolving preferences and interests, thereby enhancing the precision and relevance of recommendations. The traditional sequential recommendation algorithms are mostly based on the Markov Chain (MC) \( \left\lbrack {8,{10},{11},{39},{43}}\right\rbrack \) . It is assumed that the user's behavior sequence can be modeled as an MC, where each state represents an item and the transition probability represents the probability of the user moving from one item to another. For example, Rendle et al. [39] proposed the FPMC model, which introduces a personalized MC that relies on a personalized transfer matrix, allowing to capture both sequential user preferences and long-term user preferences. Later, He and McAuley [11] combined similarity-based models with higher-order MCs to further improve recommendation performance. Driven by the success of sequence learning in natural language processing, many researchers have started applying deep neural network-based methods to capture sequence dynamics in sequential recommendation tasks. For instance, Tang and Wang [48] introduced the Convolutional Sequence Embedding Recommendation model (Caser), which represents items in a sequence as "images" in temporal and latent spaces, utilizing convolutional filters to learn sequence patterns as local features within the image. Moreover, given the RNN's ability to effectively model variable-length sequence data, numerous RNN-based sequential recommendation algorithms have been developed. Hidasi et al. [13] were the first to apply GRU to sequential recommendation. Quadrana et al. [36] leveraged RNNs to address sequential recommendation tasks, creating a hierarchical RNN model that transfers the final evolution of the RNN's latent states across user sessions. Additionally, Hidasi and Karatzoglou [12] introduced a novel ranking loss function specifically tailored for RNNs, resulting in improved performance in sequential recommendation. Over time, self-attention [49, 52] has been introduced into sequential recommendation due to its good performance in sequence learning. For example, Kang and McAuley [16] proposed a self-attention-based sequential model (SASRec), which can both capture long-term semantics (such as RNN) and predict based on relatively few recent actions (such as MC). Sun et al. [46] proposed BERT4Rec, which introduces deep bidirectional self-attention to model user behavior sequences. In addition to the above methods, SR-GNN [53] modeled behavioral sequences as graph-structured data and utilized graph neural networks to capture complex item transitions. Chen et al. [6] designed a memory augmented neural network, which introduces the memory mechanism into the sequential recommendation. Ren et al. [37] proposed a multi-factor generative adversarial network, which introduces adversarial learning into sequential recommendation. Xin et al. [54] proposed self-supervised reinforcement learning for the sequential recommendation task. Ma et al. [27] proposed a Hierarchical Gating Network (HGN) to simultaneously capture users' long-term interests and short-term interests. And then MA-GNN [28], a memory augmented graph neural network was proposed to capture both the long- and short-term user interests. Zhang et al. [61] proposed a Graph Contrastive Learning for Sequential Recommendation (GCL4SR), which utilizes a global transition graph and graph contrastive learning to improve sequence representation learning.

### 2.3 Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation Cross-domain sequential recommendation is the combination of cross-domain recommendation and sequential recommendation. For the cross-domain sequential recommendation task, a popular solution is to model user interest representation in each single-domain separately, and then design a transferring module to transfer the representation between multiple domains. For example, \( \pi \) -Net [32], a pioneer algorithm, utilized GRUs to generate the representation of each user's behavior sequence and extracted and shared useful information cyclically between domains through the cross-domain transfer units. Then,PSJNet [47] expanded on the basis of \( \pi \) -Net and proposed a parallel split-join scheme. DA-GCN [9] first linked users and items in each domain as a graph, which builds a cross-domain sequence graph to link different domains to model complex interactions. MIFN [31] designed a behavior transfer unit and a knowledge transfer unit, taking into account both behavioral information flow and knowledge flow. Liu et al. [25] proposed a joint Internal multi-interest exploration and External domain alignment for cross-domain Sequential Recommendation model, which is a solution when users in the source and target domains do not overlap. Ma et al. [29] proposed a novel Triple Sequence Learning for Cross-Domain Recommendation (Tri-CDR) framework, which focuses on modeling the dual relationships between the source and target domains or the mixed and target domains. Lin et al. [22] also proposed a model that does not require overlapping users, which is a hybrid attention network (MAN) with local and global attention modules. Recent studies have started exploring the application of cross-domain recommendation models under open-world assumptions, addressing the limitations of closed-world settings and the challenges of data sparsity and cold-start issues on real-world platforms. AMID [56] is a framework for cross-domain sequential recommendation that addresses the challenges of open-world assumptions. It comprises a multi-interest information module and a doubly robust estimator. Xu et al. [55] proposed a Model-Agnostic Contrastive Denoising (MACD) framework for open-world cross-domain sequential recommendation. MACD leveraged auxiliary behavior sequences to uncover potential user interests, particularly for long-tail and cold-start users. It employed a denoising interest-aware network combined with a contrastive information regularizer to refine user embeddings and facilitate cross-domain knowledge transfer. In this work, we mainly focus on fusing the cross-domain interactions via a HGN to better capture both short-term and long-term user preferences across multiple domains. The techniques proposed in AMID [56] and MACD [55] can be integrated with HGNCDSR to further improve the performance for open-world problems.

Meanwhile, contrastive learning has been applied to the cross-domain sequential recommendation task. For example,Cao et al. [4] proposed \( {C}^{2} \) DSR,which utilizes a graph and attention encoder to simultaneously model intra-sequence and inter-sequence item relationships, and design two sequential objectives with contrasting objectives to jointly learn and enhance single-domain and cross-domain user preferences. Zang et al. [58] proposed CMVCDR, which is the first to apply contrastive learning to distinguish users' domain-specific and domain-invariant interests in the cross-domain sequential recommendation task. Moreover, CMVCDR designed two attention mechanisms to capture the relationship between the user's general interests and current interests. The aforementioned algorithms have demonstrated effectiveness in cross-domain sequential recommendation tasks. However, they primarily focus on modeling user preferences based solely on the most recent item interactions, overlooking the impact of long-term behavioral patterns. To address this critical limitation, we propose a HGN to capture users' current preference representations at both the feature and instance levels, separately for single-domain and cross-domain scenarios. Given that users have extensive item sequences across multiple domains over a long period, their overall representations can be learned and refined while simultaneously extracting current preference representations. Additionally, the item-item product is utilized to model the associations between candidate items and those in the behavior sequence. ## 3 Problem Definition In this work, we consider a general CDSR scenario, where each interaction sequence involves two domains,namely \( X \) and \( Y \) . Let \( \mathcal{X} \) and \( \mathcal{Y} \) denote the sets of all items in domain \( X \) and domain \( Y \) ,respectively,and let \( \mathcal{U} \) denote the set of common users from both domain \( X \) and domain \( Y \) . Common users here refer to users who have interactions in both domain \( X \) and domain \( Y \) . For each user \( u \) in \( \mathcal{U},{\mathcal{S}}_{u}^{X} = \left\lbrack {{x}_{1},{x}_{2},\ldots ,{x}_{\left| {\mathcal{S}}_{u}^{X}\right| }}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\mathcal{S}}_{u}^{Y} = \left\lbrack {{y}_{1},{y}_{2},\ldots ,{y}_{\left| {\mathcal{S}}_{u}^{Y}\right| }}\right\rbrack \) denote the chronological sequence of items that user \( u \) interacted with in domain \( X \) and domain \( Y \) respectively,and \( {\mathcal{S}}_{u}^{C} = \; \left\lbrack {{x}_{1},{y}_{1},{y}_{2},\ldots ,{x}_{\left| {\mathcal{S}}_{u}^{X}\right| },\ldots ,{y}_{\left| {\mathcal{S}}_{u}^{Y}\right| }}\right\rbrack \) denotes the item sequence in cross-domain \( C \) which is merged by \( {\mathcal{S}}_{u}^{X} \) and \( {\mathcal{S}}_{u}^{Y} \) in the chronological order. In addition, \( {x}_{i}\left( {1 \leq i \leq \left| {\mathcal{S}}_{u}^{X}\right| }\right) \) is the \( i \) th item in \( \mathcal{X} \) ,and \( {y}_{j}\left( {1 \leq j \leq \left| {\mathcal{S}}_{u}^{Y}\right| }\right) \) is the \( j \) th item in \( \mathcal{Y} \) . Given \( u \) and \( {\mathcal{S}}_{u} = \left( {{\mathcal{S}}_{u}^{X},{\mathcal{S}}_{u}^{Y},{\mathcal{S}}_{u}^{C}}\right) \) ,the aim of the cross-domain sequential recommendation task is to calculate the recommendation probability for all candidate items,and then give the final top- \( k \) recommendation list based on the probability: \[{\mathcal{P}}^{X}\left( {{x}_{i} \mid {\mathcal{S}}_{u}}\right) \sim {f}_{X}\left( {\mathcal{S}}_{u}\right) \tag{1}\] \[{\mathcal{P}}^{Y}\left( {{y}_{i} \mid {\mathcal{S}}_{u}}\right) \sim {f}_{Y}\left( {\mathcal{S}}_{u}\right) \tag{2}\] where \( {\mathcal{P}}^{X}\left( {{x}_{i} \mid {\mathcal{S}}_{u}}\right) \) and \( {\mathcal{P}}^{Y}\left( {{y}_{i} \mid {\mathcal{S}}_{u}}\right) \) represent the probability of candidate item in domain \( X \) and domain \( Y \) ,respectively,and \( {f}_{X}\left( {\mathcal{S}}_{u}\right) \) and \( {f}_{Y}\left( {\mathcal{S}}_{u}\right) \) represent the model to estimate the probabilities. Note that for user \( u \) ,we do not recommend the items that the user has already interacted with. So, the candidate items should not coincide with the items in the user's historical item sequence, which means that \( {x}_{i} \) or \( {y}_{i} \) is not an item in \( {\mathcal{S}}_{u} \) . Finally, we describe the objective function of our model in Section 4.5. ### 4.1 Overall Framework of HGNCDSR The core concept of our model is to separately extract user preferences from single-domain and cross-domain sequences, and then integrate these preferences to predict the next item the user will interact with. Specifically, we employ a HGN, comprising a feature gating module and an instance gating module, to capture user interests from single-domain and cross-domain sequences. We also utilize an item-item product to model the relationships between candidate items and those in the interaction sequence. Based on the extracted interests and item-item relationships, we calculate the ratings for all candidate items. The final item rating is obtained by summing the ratings from both single-domain and cross-domain scenarios. Ultimately,the top- \( k \) recommendation results are generated based on these combined ratings.

Based on matrix \( H \) ,the item position sequence embedding can be represented as follows: \[{P}_{i,l,D} = \left\lbrack \begin{matrix} & | & | & | & \\ \cdots & {h}_{j - 1} & {h}_{j} & {h}_{j + 1} & \cdots \\ & | & | & | & \end{matrix}\right\rbrack , \tag{4}\] where \( {P}_{i,l,D} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times \left| L\right| } \) indicates the position embedding of the \( l \) th item sequence of user \( {u}_{i} \) in domain \( D \) ,and \( {h}_{j} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d} \) is the \( j \) th column of the embedding matrix \( H \) . ### 4.3 Gating Layer We employ a gating layer to extract user interests. Recent interactions with items are crucial for reflecting a user's current preferences. Different users may prioritize different attributes of the same item based on their personal preferences. Additionally, the impact of each recent interaction on predicting future behavior varies. Ma et al. [27] addressed these issues in sequential recommendation tasks by introducing a personalized feature gating module and a personalized instance gating module, which yielded significant performance improvements. Inspired by this approach, we incorporate a personalized gating layer into our model to effectively extract user interests in the context of cross-domain sequential recommendations. In cross-domain sequential recommendation, integrating data from multiple related domains poses a challenge. Extracting user interests from item sequences in each domain separately and then merging them may overlook the temporal correlations between items across domains. Conversely, directly extracting user interests from a combined cross-domain sequence risks homogenizing distinct domains, effectively treating them as a single, uniform domain. To address these issues, HGNCDSR employs a personalized gating network for item sequences from each domain- \( X,Y \) ,and the cross-domain \( C \) . Specifically,we extract user preferences from single-domain data to preserve the unique characteristics of each domain while avoiding cross-domain influence. Simultaneously, we capture user preferences from the cross-domain sequence, utilizing information from various domains to enrich the target domain.

Fig. 4. The structure of the gating layer. It is widely assumed that recently interacted items are more reflective of a user's current interests, making the position of items within the interaction sequence crucial for predicting subsequent interactions. In traditional sequential recommendation tasks, item sequences inherently include position information within their domain. However, in cross-domain sequential recommendation tasks, item sequences span multiple domains without explicit domain markers, while single-domain sequences contain placeholders for items from other domains. To address this, we introduce item position sequences. These sequences not only represent an item's position within its domain but also differentiate items from various domains within cross-domain sequences. The structure of the final personalized gating layer, illustrated in Figure 4, consists of a feature gating module, an instance gating module, and an aggregation module. The design and functionality of each module are discussed in detail in the following sections. 4.3.1 Feature Gating. An item has many characteristics. For the same item, different users may prefer different characteristics of the item. For example, for the same movie, some people like its suspense style, while others like its starring role. The aim of the feature gating is to extract item features that reflect user's preferences and then pass them to the downstream layers. Through the feature gating module, the user's item feature-level preferences are extracted based on the item sequences in domain \( X \) ,domain \( Y \) ,and cross-domain \( C \) ,respectively. The module mechanism is related to the user representation and the item sequence. The three feature gating modules corresponding to domain \( X \) ,domain \( Y \) and cross-domain \( C \) share the mechanism at the user representation, but do not share the mechanism at the item sequence level. As shown in Equations (5)-(7),the parameter \( {W}_{{g}_{1}} \) is shared,and the parameters \( {W}_{{g}_{2}},{W}_{{g}_{3}} \) ,and \( {W}_{{g}_{4}} \) are not shared: \[{S}_{i,l,X}^{F} = {S}_{i,l,X} \otimes \sigma \left( {{W}_{{g}_{1}} \cdot {u}_{i} + {W}_{{g}_{2}} \cdot {S}_{i,l,X}}\right) \tag{5}\] \[{S}_{i,l,Y}^{F} = {S}_{i,l,Y} \otimes \sigma \left( {{W}_{{g}_{1}} \cdot {u}_{i} + {W}_{{g}_{3}} \cdot {S}_{i,l,Y}}\right) \tag{6}\] \[{S}_{i,l,C}^{F} = {S}_{i,l,C} \otimes \sigma \left( {{W}_{{g}_{1}} \cdot {u}_{i} + {W}_{{g}_{4}} \cdot {S}_{i,l,C}}\right) , \tag{7}\] where \( {u}_{i} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d} \) represents the \( i \) th column of the embedding matrix \( U,{W}_{{g}_{1}},{W}_{{g}_{2}},{W}_{{g}_{3}},{W}_{{g}_{4}} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times d} \) are learnable parameters of feature gating, \( \sigma \) is the sigmoid function, \( \otimes \) represents the element-wise product,and \( {S}_{i,l,X}^{F},{S}_{i,l,Y}^{F},{S}_{i,l,C}^{F} \) respectively represent the results of \( {S}_{i,l,X},{S}_{i,l,Y} \) ,and \( {S}_{i,l,C} \) after the feature gating processing. Through the feature gating modules, the item sequence representations filtered by item features in single-domain and cross-domain scenarios are generated.

4.3.2 Instance Gating. For the same item, different users may exhibit varying degrees of preference. For instance, among individuals who watched the same movie, some may have done so due to a strong interest, while others may have watched it out of curiosity or simply at random. The primary objective of the instance gating mechanism is to extract items that accurately reflect user preferences and then forward them to the downstream layer. The instance gate utilizes the output of the feature gate as its input. It is important to note that the instance gating is influenced not only by the user representation but also by the item position sequence. This consideration is crucial because the position of an item within its domain plays a significant role when filtering item instances. The three instance gating modules corresponding to domain \( X \) ,domain \( Y \) and cross-domain \( C \) share the mechanism at the user representation and the item position sequence, but do not share the mechanism at the item sequence level. As shown in Equations (8)-(10), the parameters \( {W}_{{g}_{5}} \) and \( {w}_{{g}_{6}} \) are shared,and the parameters \( {w}_{{g}_{7}},{w}_{{g}_{8}} \) ,and \( {w}_{{g}_{9}} \) are not shared: \[{S}_{i,l,X}^{I} = {S}_{i,l,X}^{F} \otimes \sigma \left( {{u}_{i}^{T} \cdot {W}_{{g}_{5}} + {w}_{{g}_{6}}^{T} \cdot {P}_{i,l,X} + {w}_{{g}_{7}}^{T} \cdot {S}_{i,l,X}^{F}}\right) \tag{8}\] \[{S}_{i,l,Y}^{I} = {S}_{i,l,Y}^{F} \otimes \sigma \left( {{u}_{i}^{T} \cdot {W}_{{g}_{5}} + {w}_{{g}_{6}}^{T} \cdot {P}_{i,l,Y} + {w}_{{g}_{8}}^{T} \cdot {S}_{i,l,Y}^{F}}\right) \tag{9}\] \[{S}_{i,l,C}^{I} = {S}_{i,l,C}^{F} \otimes \sigma \left( {{u}_{i}^{T} \cdot {W}_{{g}_{5}} + {w}_{{g}_{6}}^{T} \cdot {P}_{i,l,C} + {w}_{{g}_{9}}^{T} \cdot {S}_{i,l,C}^{F}}\right) , \tag{10}\] where \( {W}_{{g}_{5}} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times \left| L\right| },{w}_{{g}_{6}},{w}_{{g}_{7}},{w}_{{g}_{8}},{w}_{{g}_{9}} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d} \) are learnable parameters of instance gating,and \( {S}_{i,l,X}^{I},{S}_{i,l,Y}^{I},{S}_{i,l,C}^{I} \) respectively represent the results of \( {S}_{i,l,X}^{F},{S}_{i,l,Y}^{F} \) ,and \( {S}_{i,l,C}^{F} \) after the instance gating processing. Through the instance gating modules, the item sequence representations filtered by item features and item instances in single-domain and cross-domain scenarios are generated. 4.3.3 Aggregation. After applying the feature gating and the instance gating, we obtain filtered and weighted item sequence representations that preserve user's preferences at the item feature and instance levels. But the current output is still a collection of each processed item representation, so we need to fuse them into a group-level latent representation as the user interest representation. Here, we use average pooling to achieve this goal: \[{s}_{i,l,D}^{avg} = {avg} - \text{ pooling }\left( {S}_{i,l,D}^{I}\right) \tag{11}\] where \( {s}_{i,l,D}^{\text{ avg }} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d},D \in \{ X,Y,C\} \) . So that,based on Equation (11),we can get \( {s}_{i,l,X}^{\text{ avg }},{s}_{i,l,Y}^{\text{ avg }} \) and \( {s}_{i,l,C}^{\text{ avg }} \) as the output results of the whole gating layers, which respectively represent the user's current interests captured from domain \( X \) ,domain \( Y \) and cross-domain \( C \) item sequences. ### 4.4 Prediction Layer After applying the embedding layer and the gating layers,the candidate item embedding \( {q}_{j} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d} \) (the \( j \) th column of the candidate item embedding matrix \( Q \) ),the item sequence embedding \( {S}_{i,l,X} \) , \( {S}_{i,l,Y} \) and \( {S}_{i,l,C} \) ,and the current interest representations \( {s}_{i,l,X}^{avg},{s}_{i,l,Y}^{avg} \) and \( {s}_{i,l,C}^{avg} \) are obtained. At the prediction layer, we simultaneously combine the user interest representation obtained in the gating layer and the item correlation representation obtained by item-item product, to calculate the item ratings based on single-domain or cross-domain sequence. In HGNCDSR, the ratings of candidate items in domain \( X \) ,domain \( Y \) ,and cross-domain \( C \) are calculated separately,and the final rating of the candidate item is the sum of the single-domain and cross-domain ratings. Specifically, if the task is to predict the next item that user \( {u}_{i} \) will interact with in domain \( X \) ,the rating of user \( {u}_{i} \) on item \( {q}_{j} \) (item \( {q}_{j} \) is from domain \( X \) ) is:

\[{\widehat{r}}_{i,j} = {\widehat{r}}_{i,j,C} + {\widehat{r}}_{i,j,X}, \tag{12}\] Fig. 5. The structure of the prediction layer. Take the task of predicting the user's next interaction in domain \( X \) as an example. where \( {\widehat{r}}_{i,j,C} \) represents the rating of user \( {u}_{i} \) on item \( {q}_{j} \) in cross-domain \( C,{\widehat{r}}_{i,j,X} \) represents the rating of user \( {u}_{i} \) on item \( {q}_{j} \) in domain \( X \) . Otherwise,if the task is to predict the next item that user \( {u}_{i} \) will interact with in domain \( Y \) ,the rating of user \( {u}_{i} \) on item \( {q}_{j} \) (item \( {q}_{j} \) from domain \( Y \) ) is: \[{\widehat{r}}_{i,j} = {\widehat{r}}_{i,j,C} + {\widehat{r}}_{i,j,Y}, \tag{13}\] where \( {\widehat{r}}_{i,j,Y} \) represents the rating of user \( {u}_{i} \) on item \( {q}_{j} \) in domain \( Y \) . At the prediction layer,the prediction unit is used to calculate \( {\widehat{r}}_{i,j,D}\left( {D \in \{ X,Y,C\} }\right) \) . When predicting a user's next interaction, the user's current interests and the correlation between items should be taken into consideration simultaneously. The rating of a candidate item consists of two parts: the rating for the candidate item based on the user's current interests, and the correlation rating between the candidate item and the items the user has recently interacted with. Here, we utilize the output of the gating layer to model user's interests, and use the product of sequence item embedding and candidate item embedding to model item association relationships. For example, given the \( l \) th sequence to predict,the rating of user \( {u}_{i} \) on item \( {q}_{j} \) in domain \( D \) is: \[{\widehat{r}}_{i,j,D} = {s}_{i,j,D}^{avg} \cdot {q}_{j} + \left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{{e}_{k} \in {S}_{i,l,D}}}{e}_{k}^{T} \cdot {q}_{j}}\right) /\left| L\right| . \tag{14}\] Finally, we can provide users with cross-domain sequential recommendation results for domain \( X \) and domain \( Y \) based on the final candidate item ratings. The task of predicting an item in domain \( Y \) is similar. ### 4.5 Objective Function In HGNCDSR, we employ the Bayesian Personalized Ranking objective function [38] to train our model, which means optimizing the pairwise ranking between the positive items and negative items. The positive items here refer to the items that the users actually interact with in the next step, while the negative items are randomly selected from the items that the users have not interacted with. Since we simultaneously train item sequences from domain \( X \) ,domain \( Y \) ,and cross-domain \( C \) scenarios, and calculate the ratings of candidate items respectively, each single-domain training process and cross-domain training process require a specific loss function for optimization. The loss function for domain \( X \) ,domain \( Y \) ,or cross-domain \( C \) training process can be uniformly expressed by the following equation:

\[{L}_{D}\left( {U,Q,E,{\Theta }_{D}}\right) = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\left( {i,j,k}\right) \in \mathfrak{D}}} - \log \sigma \left( {{\widehat{r}}_{i,j,D} - {\widehat{r}}_{i,k,D}}\right) + \mu \left( {\parallel U{\parallel }^{2} + \parallel Q{\parallel }^{2} + \parallel E{\parallel }^{2} + {\begin{Vmatrix}{\Theta }_{D}\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}}\right) , \tag{15}\] where \( j \) denotes the ground truth item, \( k \) denotes the negative item sampled randomly, \( {\Theta }_{D} \) represents all parameters of the gating layer in domain \( D \) ,and \( \mu \) represents the regularization parameter. According to Equation (15),loss functions \( {L}_{X}\left( {U,Q,E,{\Theta }_{X}}\right) ,{L}_{Y}\left( {U,Q,E,{\Theta }_{Y}}\right) \) ,and \( {L}_{C}\left( {U,Q,E,{\Theta }_{C}}\right) \) are obtained. Then, we proposed the final loss function in HGNCDSR: \[L\left( {U,Q,E,\Theta }\right) = \lambda {L}_{C}\left( {U,Q,E,{\Theta }_{C}}\right) + \left( {1 - \lambda }\right) \left( {{L}_{X}\left( {U,Q,E,{\Theta }_{X}}\right) + {L}_{Y}\left( {U,Q,E,{\Theta }_{Y}}\right) }\right) , \tag{16}\] where \( \Theta \) represents all parameters in the gating layer and \( \lambda \) is a hyperparameter used to adjust the weighted proportion of loss function in single-domain and cross-domain. Then, all parameters can be learned by minimizing \( L\left( {U,Q,E,\Theta }\right) \) in an end-to-end back-propagation training way. ## 5 Experiments In this section, we present a comprehensive set of experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of HGNCDSR using three real-world datasets. ### 5.2 Evaluation Metrics Previous works [4, 16, 46, 63] have extensively utilized the leave-one-out method to evaluate recommendation performance, so here we also follow the convention. The leave-one-out method refers to using the user's last real interaction as the recommendation target. At the same time, we adopt the scheme proposed by Rendle's literature [18], which randomly samples 999 negative items, plus one positive item, thereby calculating 1,000 scores for each verification or test case. In our experiments, we utilize three evaluation metrics commonly used in the field of recommendation systems to measure model performance, namely Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR), Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG), and Hit Ratio (HR). MRR considers the ranking quality of real values in the recommendation list. The higher the ranking, the higher the MRR value, indicating the better the performance of the recommendation system. The formula for calculating MRR is as follows: \[{MRR} = \frac{1}{V}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{V}\frac{1}{\operatorname{ran}{k}_{i}} \tag{17}\] where \( V \) represents the number of validation or test cases,and \( {\operatorname{rank}}_{i} \) represents the position of the ground truth of the \( i \) th test case in the recommendation list. NDCG@ \( k \) is used to measure the ranking quality of real values in the top- \( k \) recommendation list: \[{NDCG}@k = \frac{1}{V}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{V}\frac{\log 2}{\log \left( {{\operatorname{rank}}_{i} + 1}\right) }. \tag{18}\] HR@ \( k \) focuses on whether the top- \( k \) recommendation list contains items that the user actually likes: \[{HR}@k = \frac{1}{V}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{V}\delta \left( {{\operatorname{rank}}_{i} < k}\right) , \tag{19}\] where \( \delta \left( \cdot \right) \) denotes the indicator function. In our experiments,when evaluating NDCG, \( k \) is set to \( \{ 5,{10}\} \) . While when evaluating HR, \( k \) is set to \( \{ 1,5,{10}\} \) . ### 5.3 Baseline Methods Due to the cross-domain sequential recommendation task, to better prove the excellent performance of HGNCDSR, we design four types of comparison methods, including traditional recommendation, cross-domain recommendation, sequential recommendation, and cross-domain sequential recommendation.

5.3.1 Traditional Recommendations. Traditional recommendation algorithms only focus on the three dimensions of users, items, and users' ratings of items, without considering other additional information, such as time order, domain sources, and so on. For traditional recommendation algorithms, we choose two classic models as baselines: - BPRMF [38]: It combines the ideas of Bayesian Personalized Ranking and Matrix Factorization. On the one hand, it is based on Bayesian Personalized Ranking, that is, using pairwise comparisons during the training process to learn the user's preferences for items. On the other hand, it uses Matrix Factorization to represent users and items as low-dimensional vectors, capturing the similarity and correlation information between users and items. - ItemKNN [41]: It is a collaborative filtering recommendation algorithm based on items, which recommends items to users by computing the similarity between items. Its main idea is to find other items similar to the target item based on users' historical behavior data. When using the two traditional recommendation algorithms as baselines for comparison with HGNCDSR, we treat the two related domains as a single domain and disregard the temporal order of user interactions. 5.3.2 Cross-Domain Recommendations. Cross-domain recommendation algorithms utilize the user's historical behavior data from multiple domains to model user interests and recommend items in the target domain to the user. For cross-domain recommendation algorithms, we choose the following two models as baselines: - EMCDR [33]: It is a classic cross-domain recommendation algorithm that uses multi-layer perceptron to simulate the cross-domain nonlinear mapping function. - CoNet [14]: It is a well-known cross-domain recommendation algorithm. It builds a neural network for each domain, and the networks in each domain exchange information and learn collaboratively by sharing some parameters or through a common embedding space. In our experiments, the two aforementioned cross-domain recommendation algorithms only account for cross-domain scenarios without considering the chronological information of interaction records. 5.3.3 Sequential Recommendations. Sequential recommendation algorithms arrange the user's historical interactions belonging to a certain domain into item sequences in chronological order, and predict the user's next interaction based on the item sequence. We use the following three sequential recommendation algorithms as the baselines for our experiments: - SASRec [16]: It is a recommendation algorithm for processing sequential recommendation tasks, which utilizes the self-attention mechanism to capture sequential patterns and dependencies in user-item interactions. -HGN [27]: It is a single-domain sequential recommendation algorithm, which is the most relevant one to our model. This algorithm is based on single-domain data and uses a gating network to extract user's current feature-level and instance-level preferences, while taking into account the user's long-term interests and the correlation between items. - GCL4SR [61]: It constructs a weighted item transition graph from all users' behavior sequences to offer a comprehensive view of item transition patterns. For each user's interaction sequence, it randomly samples two subgraphs to generate global context information. Additionally, it employs contrastive learning to ensure that the representations of identical sequences are similar.

Our model builds on HGN by designing a framework and modifying the gating module to extend the algorithm's application from single-domain to cross-domain scenarios. For the three sequential recommendation algorithms mentioned above, we treat the two related domains as a single domain, with interaction data arranged in chronological order. 5.3.4 Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendations. Cross-domain sequential recommendation algorithms are equivalent to the combination of cross-domain recommendation and sequence recommendation, taking into account domain information and time sequence information. Here, we take the following four cross-domain sequential recommendation algorithms as baselines: - \( \pi \) -net [32]: It is a pioneer algorithm in the field of cross-domain sequential recommendation, which designs a cross-domain transfer unit to realize information transfer between domains. - PSJNet [47]: It is extended based on \( \pi \) -net and introduces a parallel split-join scheme to achieve better performance. \( - {C}^{2}{DSR} \) [4]: It is a well-known cross-domain sequential recommendation algorithm with good performance in recent years. It considers both inter-sequence and intra-sequence item relationships. First, a graph neural network is used to mine item collaboration relationships between sequences, and then a sequential attention encoder is used to capture item order relationships within a sequence. Moreover, contrastive learning is introduced to better learn user interest representation. - Tri-CDR [29]: It is one of the state-of-the-art CDR models that conducts a triple cross-domain attention method to highlight useful information and accelerate positive knowledge transfer, and enables a more accurate multi-domain sequence representation learning strategy via both the coarse-grained similarity modeling and fine-grained distinction modeling. ### 5.4 Experiment Settings In our experiments, for sequential recommendation and cross-domain sequential recommendation, we follow the data processing method in \( {C}^{2} \) DSR. The maximum item sequence length is set to 15 for the Food-Kitchen, Movie-Book, and Sports-Clothing cross-domain scenarios, while it is set to 30 for the Entertainment-Education cross-domain scenario. If the item sequence length is less than the maximum length, 0 is used as the padding value. 5.5.1 Considering Domain Information Can Help Improve Recommendation Performance. We selected two traditional recommendation algorithms and two cross-domain recommendation algorithms as baselines. By comparing the experimental performance of these two types of methods, we can find that the overall performance of EMCDR and CoNet models is better than that of BPRMF and ItemKNN models. Here we try to analyze the reason for this phenomenon. In our experiments, both the traditional recommendation models and the cross-domain recommendation models applied the same amount of interaction data. The difference is that the traditional recommendation models treat two different domains as the same domain, while the cross-domain recommendation models process the data of the two domains separately, and then transfer the learned representations between domains. The experimental results illustrate that when predicting the next interaction in a certain domain, it is not appropriate to treat this domain and another domain equally. 5.5.2 Considering Chronological Information Can Help Improve Recommendation Performance. In our experiment, three sequential recommendation models were also selected as baselines. According to the experimental results, compared with the traditional recommendation models, the sequential recommendation models, SASRec, HGN, and GCL4SR have better recommendation performance. The reason for this phenomenon is that traditional recommendation models treat interaction data from different time periods equally, whereas sequential recommendation models are trained on interaction sequences organized chronologically. As a result, traditional algorithms can only capture users' general interests, while sequential recommendation algorithms can model user interests specific to particular time periods. Since user interests evolve dynamically over time, sequential recommendation methods are better equipped to capture these changes. 5.5.3 Hierarchical Gated Networks Can Capture User Interests Well. HGN [27] is an algorithm proposed by Ma et al. in 2019 [27] that uses HGNs to solve the sequential recommendation task. It can be observed from Table 3 that HGN outperforms some other baseline algorithms (even cross-domain sequential recommendation algorithms in some cases) on many evaluation metrics. The good recommendation performance of the HGN proves the advantages of hierarchical gated networks in extracting user interest representations. Our model, HGNCDSR, is designed and improved on the basis of HGN, extending the idea of using hierarchical gated networks to model user interests to the cross-domain sequential recommendation scenario. Therefore, this observation lays the foundation for the good performance of our model. 5.5.4 Our Model Can Achieve Better Results Than the Baseline Models on Many Evaluation Metrics. The experimental results are shown in Figure 6. The five models of our ablation experiments are as follows: - HGNCDSR_F: It is a variant model that only applies the feature gating. Since there is no instance gating, the output of the feature gating is directly fused into a group-level latent representation through average pooling. At the prediction layer, the item-item product is not used to model correlations between items.

-HGNCDSR_I: It is a variant model that skips the feature gating and directly uses the item sequence representation as the input of instance gating. Similarly, at the prediction layer, the item-item product is not used to model the correlation between items. -HGNCDSR_G: It uses a complete gating network including feature gating and instance gating. Specifically, it applies the feature gating and the instance gating in sequence in the gating layer, but in the prediction layer, only the user's current interest representation extracted in the gating layer is used to calculate the candidate item rating, and the item-item product is not used for modeling the relationship between items. - HGNCDSR_noPos: It uses a complete gating network including feature gating and instance gating, which uses item-item products to model the correlation between items based on HGNCDSR_G. The inputs of our embedding layer only include the user id, the candidate items, the item sequence the user interacted with. Specifically, the position sequence corresponding to the item sequence is not used as inputs to the embedding layer. -HGNCDSR: It is the final model we proposed. Based on the above four models, HGNCDSR utilizes the item position sequence to distinguish the items in the cross-domain, and takes into account the influence of the user's current interests and the correlation between items in predicting the user's next interaction at the same time in the prediction layer. In the "Food-kitchen" cross-domain scenario, the recommendation performance of the above five models is shown in Figure 6. It can be observed that under most metrics, the recommendation performance of HGNCDSR_G that applies the complete gating layer network is better than HGNCDSR_F that only applies the feature gating, proving the effectiveness of the instance gating module. Similarly, the recommendation performance of HGNCDSR_G is better than that of HGNCDSR_I which only applies the instance gating, proving the effectiveness of the feature gating module. Moreover, in most cases, the recommendation performance of HGNCDSR_I is better than that of HGNCDSR_F, which shows that the instance gating module is more effective than the feature gating module in extracting the user's current interest representation. However, it should be noted that feature gating and instance gating extract user preferences at two different levels: item features and item instances respectively. So the feature gating and the instance gating can complement each other. Then, by comparing the recommendation performance of HGNCDSR and HGNCDSR_G, we found that HGNCDSR performs better than HGNCDSR_G in most metrics. Compared with HGNCDSR_G, HGNCDSR has one more step, which is to use the item-item product in the prediction layer to simulate the similarity between candidate items and items in the interaction sequence. Next, by comparing HGNCDSR and HGNCDSR_noPos, it can be observed that HGNCDSR outperforms HGNCDSR_noPos across all metrics. This indicates that when filtering item instances, it is necessary to consider the positional information of the items within their corresponding domains. The item position sequence has a significant impact on predicting the user's next interaction. ### 5.7 Framework Rationality Analysis There are two main issues for cross-domain sequential recommendation. One is how to extract user interest representations from user behavior sequences to achieve sequential recommendations and the other is how to apply user behavior data from different related domains to achieve cross-domain recommendations. To achieve the sequential recommendation task, HGNCDSR utilizes the HGN to model the user's current interests based on the user's recent item sequence. To achieve the cross-domain recommendation task, HGNCDSR simultaneously constructs and jointly trains each single-domain sequence and cross-domain sequence, calculates item ratings based on the single-domain sequence and the cross-domain sequence respectively, and sums them up at the prediction layer to obtain the final recommendation results. The motivations for the design of our model framework are detailed below. First, by merging data from different single domains in chronological order to construct a cross-domain sequence, we can effectively link the data from the two domains, thereby providing a more accurate reflection of the user's interactive behavior. The experimental results of the three sequential recommendation models (SASRec, HGN, and GCL4SR) in Table 3 can prove that using the merged interaction sequence to extract the user's interest representation is a feasible and effective method. However, extracting user interests based solely on the cross-domain sequence will ignore the differences between the two single domains. For example,one task is to recommend items from domain \( X \) to the user. At this time,the historical interaction records from domain \( X \) can better reflect the user’s preferences in this domain,while the information from domain \( Y \) only plays a supplementary role. Therefore, in our model, when training cross-domain sequences, single-domain sequences are trained at the same time to correct the overall recommendation results. To evaluate the effectiveness of simultaneous training on single-domain and cross-domain sequences, we design and implement four groups of experiments for four cross-domain scenarios of "Food-Kitchen," "Movie-Book," "Sports-Clothing," and "Entertainment-Education." We design a variant model of HGNCDSR named HGNCDSR_C. The HGNCDSR_C model only applies the HGN to the cross-domain item sequence to extract user interest representation, and the rating of the candidate item in the cross-domain scenario will be used as the final rating of the item. The experimental results in four cross-domain scenarios are shown in Figure 7, respectively. According to the results in the figures, we can observe that under most evaluation metrics, the recommendation performance of HGNCDSR has been significantly improved compared to HGNCDSR_C. This illustrates the rationality of our model training both single-domain sequences and cross-domain sequences. ### 5.8 Sparsity Study In this section, we evaluate the performance of HGNCDSR using different proportions of the training data (20%, 50%, 80%, and 100%) to examine the impact of data sparsity on model performance. To isolate the effects, we vary one hyperparameter at a time while keeping the others fixed at their optimal values. 5.9.1 Impact of the Loss Weight \( \lambda \) . In HGNCDSR,we jointly train single-domain and cross-domain sequences and calculate candidate item ratings in single-domain and cross-domain separately. Therefore, the overall loss function includes two parts, corresponding to single-domain and cross-domain scenarios,as shown in Equation (16). Here \( \lambda \) is the loss weight hyperparameter,which can adjust the proportion of the single-domain loss and the cross-domain loss during the training process. We design and implement three groups of experiments based on the three cross-domain recommendation scenarios of "Food-kitchen," "Movie-Book," and "Entertainment-Education" to analyze the impact of different values of the hyperparameter \( \lambda \) on the recommendation performance of HGNCDSR. In this experiment,the value of \( \lambda \) is set to0.2,0.4,0.6,and 0.8,respectively. The results of the recommendation performance of HGNCDSR changing with the change of hyperparameter \( \lambda \) in three cross-domain recommendation scenarios are shown in Figure 9 respectively. We count the experimental results of the three evaluation metrics: MRR, NDCG@5, and HR@1.For the "Food-Kitchen" scenario, it can be observed that when the value of \( \lambda \) is 0.8,the recommendation performance is the best. Similarly, for the "Movie-Book" scenario, the recommendation performance is optimal when the value of \( \lambda \) is 0.8 . For the above two cross-domain recommendation scenarios, the overall trend is that the recommendation performance improves as the value of \( \lambda \) increases. For the "Entertainment-Education" scenario,when the value of \( \lambda \) is 0.6, HGNCDSR achieves the best recommendation performance. And the general trend is that the recommendation performance first increases with the increase of \( \lambda \) value,and then decreases after reaching the peak value. Next, we try to analyze the phenomena observed above. As shown in Equation (16), the hyperparameter \( \lambda \) is used to balance the single-domain BPR loss and the cross-domain BPR loss. When \( \lambda \) takes a larger value,the proportion of cross-domain loss in the training process is larger, which means that the model pays more attention to extracting user interests based on cross-domain interaction sequences. Otherwise,when \( \lambda \) takes a smaller value,the proportion of single-domain loss in the training process is larger, which means that the model pays more attention to extracting user interests based on single-domain interaction sequences. And it should be noted that the single-domain BPR loss consists of two parts,namely the BPR loss in domain \( X \) and the BPR loss in domain Y. This means that the value of single-domain BPR loss will be greater than the value of cross-domain BPR loss. Therefore, according to common sense, when the recommendation performance reaches its peak,the value of the hyperparameter \( \lambda \) should take a relatively large number. The phenomena shown in the experimental results in Figure 9, are in line with the basic expectations of our HGNCDSR model.

Our approach acknowledges that a user's next interaction is influenced by both their general behavior patterns and their recent interests. To capture these dynamics, we employ a gating mechanism that integrates user representations to reflect current interests effectively. By leveraging long-term historical interaction sequences across multiple domains, our model strengthens the user representation, thereby capturing both general behavior patterns and domain-specific preferences. HGNCDSR trains on both single-domain and cross-domain item sequences, allowing for the integration of domain-specific insights while enhancing connections between related domains. During the prediction phase, we utilize item-item products to model item correlations, thereby refining candidate item ratings based on both current user interests and item relationships. Extensive experiments validate the superiority and effectiveness of our approach.
